title: Wildlife You Can See in Kuno National Park
author: Nived Yadav
excerpt: Kuno National Park is one of the most diverse wildlife destinations in Central India. While it is internationally known as the home of India's African cheetahs, the park supports a rich ecosystem of predators, herbivores, reptiles and more than 200 species of birds...
content: Kuno National Park is one of the most diverse wildlife destinations in Central India. While it is internationally known as the home of India's African cheetahs, the park supports a rich ecosystem of predators, herbivores, reptiles and more than 200 species of birds. The park's unique mix of open grasslands, dry deciduous forests, riverine habitats and rocky hills creates ideal conditions for a wide variety of wildlife. Every safari is different, and visitors never know what they may encounter around the next corner. Here's a closer look at the incredible wildlife you can expect to see during your safari in Kuno National Park. Big Cats of Kuno National Park Kuno National Park is one of the few wildlife destinations in India where visitors can search for three iconic big cats—the African Cheetah, Leopard and Tiger. The park is also home to one of India's rarest wild cats, the elusive Caracal. Together, these magnificent predators make Kuno one of the country's most exciting safari destinations for wildlife lovers and photographers. {{image:1}} 🐆 African Cheetah The African Cheetah is the biggest attraction of Kuno National Park and the flagship species of Project Cheetah. Reintroduced to India in 2022 after being extinct in the country for over 70 years, cheetahs have adapted well to Kuno's grasslands and open forests. Visitors often search for them resting under trees, scanning the grasslands or hunting prey like chital and chinkara. Kuno is currently the only place in India where you can see free-ranging African cheetahs in the wild. {{image:2}} 🐆 Leopard Leopards are among the most frequently sighted large carnivores in Kuno National Park. Their excellent camouflage allows them to blend seamlessly into rocky hills, forests and grasslands. Unlike cheetahs, leopards rely on stealth and strength to hunt. Early morning and evening safaris often provide excellent opportunities to spot these beautiful cats walking along forest tracks or resting on rocky outcrops. {{image:3}} 🐅 Tiger Kuno is also home to Bengal Tigers, making it one of the rare places in India where three iconic big cats share the same landscape. Although tiger sightings are currently less frequent than those of cheetahs and leopards, their presence represents another major milestone in Kuno's conservation journey. As the tiger population grows, sightings are expected to become more common in the coming years. {{image:4}} 🦊 Caracal The Caracal is one of India's rarest and most elusive wild cats. Recognised by its distinctive black ear tufts and reddish coat, it inhabits dry grasslands and scrub forests within the Kuno landscape. Sightings are exceptionally rare, but the presence of this secretive feline highlights the incredible biodiversity of Kuno National Park and makes it a dream destination for serious wildlife enthusiasts. {{image:5}} Predators & Bears of Kuno National Park Beyond its famous big cats, Kuno supports several other fascinating predators that play an important role in maintaining the park's ecological balance. 🐻 Sloth Bear Sloth Bears are regularly seen in Kuno, especially near rocky hills and termite mounds. With their shaggy black coat and long claws, they spend much of their time searching for insects, fruits and honey. Watching a sloth bear foraging in the wild is always a memorable safari experience. {{image:6}} 🐺 Indian Wolf The Indian Wolf is one of Kuno's most elusive predators. Adapted to open grasslands and scrub habitats, wolves are usually seen during the cooler hours of the day. Although sightings are uncommon, encountering one in the wild is considered a special moment for any wildlife enthusiast. {{image:7}} 🐕 Dhole (Indian Wild Dog) The Dhole, or Indian Wild Dog, is an intelligent and highly social predator that hunts in coordinated packs. Though not commonly seen, they occasionally move through Kuno's forests in search of prey. Their teamwork and endurance make them one of India's most effective hunters. {{image:8}} 🐺 Striped Hyena Striped Hyenas are mostly active during the evening and night but are occasionally seen during safaris. As nature's cleanup crew, they play a vital role by scavenging carcasses and keeping the ecosystem healthy. {{image:9}} 🦊 Golden Jackal Golden Jackals are among the most commonly seen carnivores in Kuno. They are highly adaptable and can often be spotted alone or in pairs near grasslands and forest edges. Their distinctive calls are frequently heard during dawn and dusk. {{image:10}} Herbivores of Kuno National Park Kuno's healthy population of herbivores forms the foundation of its ecosystem and provides food for predators like cheetahs, leopards and tigers. 🦌 Chital (Spotted Deer) Chital are the most abundant deer species in Kuno National Park. Their loud alarm calls often alert guides to the presence of predators nearby, making them an important part of every safari. {{image:11}} 🦌 Sambar India's largest deer species, the Sambar prefers dense forests and areas close to water. Their deep alarm calls are a reliable sign that a predator may be in the vicinity. {{image:12}} 🦌 Chinkara (Indian Gazelle) The graceful Chinkara thrives in Kuno's open grasslands and is one of the preferred prey species of the African cheetah. They are often seen moving gracefully across open plains. {{image:13}} 🐃 Nilgai (Blue Bull) The Nilgai is Asia's largest antelope and one of the most frequently encountered herbivores in Kuno. These majestic animals are commonly seen grazing in open grasslands throughout the park. {{image:14}} 🐗 Wild Boar Wild Boars are widespread across Kuno National Park and are frequently observed foraging near forest roads and water bodies. They are an important food source for the park's large predators. {{image:15}} Reptiles of Kuno National Park Kuno's rivers, wetlands and forests also support an impressive diversity of reptiles. 🐊 Mugger Crocodile The Mugger Crocodile is commonly found in the Kuno River and other permanent water bodies within the park. Visitors often spot them basking on riverbanks during sunny afternoons. {{image:16}} 🐊 Gharial The Kuno River is also home to the Critically Endangered Gharial, one of the world's rarest crocodilians. Easily recognised by its long, narrow snout, the gharial is a fish-eating reptile and an important part of Kuno's aquatic ecosystem. Spotting one during a safari is a special experience for wildlife enthusiasts. {{image:17}} Birds of Kuno National Park With more than 200 recorded bird species, Kuno National Park is a paradise for birdwatchers. From majestic birds of prey to colourful woodland species, every safari offers excellent birding opportunities throughout the year. 🦉 Forest Owlet One of Kuno's greatest birding attractions is the Forest Owlet, one of India's rarest owl species. Once believed to be extinct, it is now one of the most sought-after birds for birdwatchers and wildlife photographers visiting Central India. {{image:18}} Other Birds You May See Kuno National Park is home to an incredible variety of resident and migratory birds, including: White-eyed Buzzard Crested Serpent Eagle Changeable Hawk-Eagle Indian Eagle-Owl Painted Spurfowl Indian Peafowl Paradise Flycatcher Indian Roller Green Bee-eater Kingfishers Woodpeckers Vultures Drongos Minivets Orioles Sunbirds Herons and Egrets Seasonal migratory waterbirds Whether you're a casual birdwatcher or an experienced birder, every safari in Kuno offers the chance to discover something new.

title: Safari Zones & Entry Gates in Kuno National Park
author: Nived Yadav
excerpt: If you're visiting Kuno for the first time, selecting the right gate can significantly improve both your comfort and your chances of memorable wildlife sightings...
content: Kuno National Park currently offers safari access through three tourism zones, each providing a unique landscape and wildlife experience. These are: Ahera Gate Tiktoli Gate Peepalbawri Gate Although all three gates provide access to Kuno's wilderness, the safari experience differs considerably depending on the zone you choose. Factors such as road connectivity, terrain, wildlife movement, accommodation availability and safari vehicle options can all influence your overall experience. If you're visiting Kuno for the first time, selecting the right gate can significantly improve both your comfort and your chances of memorable wildlife sightings. 1. Ahera Gate – Our Top Recommendation ⭐ If someone asks our team which safari gate they should choose, our answer is almost always Ahera Gate. Located on the Pohri side of Kuno National Park, Ahera offers the best overall combination of wildlife sightings, road connectivity and visitor convenience. It is the closest gate for most travellers arriving from Gwalior Airport, Shivpuri Railway Station and Gwalior Junction, making it the easiest gate to reach. {{image:1}} Over the past two tourism seasons, our team has spent hundreds of days tracking wildlife in this zone. Based on our field experience, Ahera has consistently produced the highest number of cheetah and leopard sightings among the three tourism gates. The zone includes a mix of open grasslands, dry deciduous forests and riverine patches, creating excellent habitat for cheetahs, leopards, sloth bears, deer and numerous bird species. Another major advantage is flexibility. Unlike Tiktoli, visitors entering through Ahera can currently choose between a registered safari Gypsy or an eligible private vehicle, subject to Forest Department rules. (bandhavgarh) Why Choose Ahera? ✅ Best road connectivity ✅ Closest to most hotels and homestays ✅ Easy access from Gwalior and Shivpuri ✅ Excellent habitat for cheetahs and leopards ✅ Suitable for first-time visitors ✅ Ideal for wildlife photographers If you're planning only one or two safaris, Ahera is the gate we recommend the most. 2. Tiktoli Gate Tiktoli was one of the original tourism gates developed for Kuno National Park and offers visitors a completely different safari experience. The landscape here consists of beautiful forests, rolling hills and open woodland, making it a wonderful area for exploring Kuno's natural beauty. Visitors frequently encounter deer, nilgai, wild boar, jackals, hyenas and a rich diversity of birds. However, based on our team's experience during recent safari seasons, cheetah sightings in this zone have generally been less frequent than at Ahera. Leopard sightings are also comparatively lower, although wildlife movement can change over time as animals expand their territories. Another important point is that only registered safari Gypsies are currently permitted from Tiktoli Gate, making advance vehicle arrangements essential. (The Times of India) Accommodation options around Tiktoli are also more limited compared to the Ahera side. {{image:2}} Tiktoli is best for: Visitors interested in exploring a quieter part of Kuno. Nature lovers who enjoy forest landscapes. Birdwatchers. Guests staying near the Tiktoli side of the park. 3. Peepalbawri Gate Peepalbawri Gate provides access to another beautiful section of Kuno National Park. The route passes through rural villages and interior roads before reaching the safari gate. While the journey offers glimpses of the local countryside, road conditions can be rough in some stretches, particularly after the monsoon. {{image:3}} Compared to Ahera, tourism infrastructure around Peepalbawri is still developing. Visitors may find fewer accommodation options and limited availability of safari Gypsies near the gate. Many guests therefore arrange their vehicles in advance before arriving. Like Ahera, eligible private vehicles are currently permitted, subject to Forest Department regulations. (The Times of India) Because comparatively fewer tourists currently enter through this gate, there is less consistent visitor data regarding wildlife sightings. However, the landscapes are beautiful and the zone has good potential as tourism continues to develop. Which Safari Gate Should You Choose? Choosing the right safari gate depends on your priorities, but based on our experience of operating in Kuno throughout the tourism season, we generally recommend: Choose Ahera Gate if you're visiting Kuno for the first time, want the best road connectivity and are primarily hoping to see cheetahs or leopards. Choose Tiktoli Gate if you're interested in exploring quieter forest landscapes and don't mind travelling in a registered Gypsy. Choose Peepalbawri Gate if you're looking to experience a less-visited part of Kuno and are comfortable travelling through rural roads. At Finding Fauna, we help our guests select the most suitable gate based on the latest wildlife movement, seasonal conditions and their travel plans, ensuring every safari has the best possible chance of becoming a memorable experience.

title: Safari Booking System in Kuno National Park
author: Nived Yadav
excerpt: Currently, Gypsy Safari is the only official safari option available inside Kuno National Park. Visitors can explore the park through three tourism zones—Ahera Gate, Tiktoli Gate, and Peepalbawri Gate—each offering different safari routes
content: Currently, Gypsy Safari is the only official safari option available inside Kuno National Park. Unlike some other tiger reserves, canter safaris are not available. At present, tourists can explore the park through three tourism zones: Ahera Gate Tiktoli Gate Peepalbawri Gate Each gate provides access to different safari routes and landscapes, offering visitors unique wildlife experiences. One important thing to know before planning your trip is that the Forest Department currently issues only the safari permit. The government booking portal does not assign a safari vehicle (Gypsy) with your permit. This means visitors must separately arrange a registered safari Gypsy through an authorised local safari operator such as Finding Fauna. Our team takes care of the complete process—from arranging the permit and safari vehicle to providing an experienced driver and guide—making your visit completely hassle-free. Visitors entering through Ahera and Peepalbawri also have the option of using their own private vehicle, subject to the latest Forest Department guidelines and permissions. However, for the best wildlife experience, especially if you're visiting for the first time, we highly recommend opting for a registered safari Gypsy with an experienced driver and naturalist. What is the Safari Experience Like? A typical safari in Kuno lasts around 3.5 to 4 hours, giving visitors ample time to explore the park's diverse habitats. {{image:1}} As your vehicle enters the forest, the landscape changes constantly. One moment you may be driving through dense Kardhai forests, and the next you could be crossing vast open grasslands where cheetahs are often seen scanning the horizon. Seasonal streams, rocky plateaus, river crossings and dry deciduous woodland create an ever-changing backdrop throughout the safari. The excitement comes from never knowing what awaits around the next bend. You might witness a cheetah resting beneath a tree, a leopard silently walking along a forest track, a sloth bear searching for termites, or a herd of chital suddenly raising alarm calls as a predator approaches. For photographers, Kuno offers exceptional opportunities thanks to its open landscapes and natural light. Unlike many forests where vegetation is extremely dense, several parts of Kuno allow for unobstructed wildlife viewing, making it easier to observe and photograph animals in their natural habitat. Every safari tells a different story—and that's what keeps visitors coming back. What Makes Kuno National Park Different? Kuno National Park is unlike any other wildlife destination in India. {{image:2}} The biggest reason, of course, is that it is the only national park in India where visitors can see free-ranging African cheetahs in the wild. Watching the world's fastest land animal thriving once again in India's forests is a truly unique experience. But Kuno's appeal goes far beyond Project Cheetah. The park is one of the very few places in India where visitors have the opportunity to search for three iconic big cats—the cheetah, the leopard, and the tiger. While tiger sightings are currently less frequent than those of cheetahs and leopards, their presence adds another exciting dimension to the safari experience. Kuno is also distinguished by its remarkably varied landscape. Instead of endless dense forest, the park features a beautiful mosaic of open grasslands, rolling hills, dry deciduous forests, riverine habitats and rocky escarpments. This diversity supports an equally rich variety of wildlife and creates a safari experience that feels different with every route you explore. Another feature that sets Kuno apart is the relatively lower tourist traffic compared to many of India's more established national parks. This allows visitors to enjoy a quieter, more immersive safari without large numbers of vehicles surrounding every wildlife sighting. {{image:3,4,5}} Why We Recommend Booking Multiple Safaris One of the most common questions we receive is: "Is one safari enough?" The simple answer is no—especially if your goal is to experience the true diversity of Kuno National Park. Kuno has an extensive tourism area, with each safari route passing through different habitats and offering different wildlife opportunities. On one drive, you may spend most of your time exploring open grasslands in search of cheetahs. On another, you could be tracking a leopard through dense woodland or watching sloth bears foraging near rocky outcrops. Wildlife is constantly on the move, and every safari unfolds differently depending on the season, weather conditions and animal behaviour. Based on our experience guiding visitors in Kuno, we generally recommend: 1 Safari – Ideal if you're short on time and simply want to experience Kuno for the first time. 2–3 Safaris – Perfect for most visitors, allowing you to explore different routes and significantly improve your chances of memorable wildlife sightings. 4–6 Safaris – Highly recommended for wildlife photographers, filmmakers and enthusiasts who want the best opportunities to observe cheetahs, leopards and other species under varying light and habitat conditions. The beauty of Kuno lies in its unpredictability. Every safari offers a fresh opportunity to witness something extraordinary, which is why many visitors leave wishing they had booked one more drive.

title: Kuno National Park Overview & History
author: Nived Yadav
excerpt: In December 2018, Kuno Wildlife Sanctuary was officially upgraded to Kuno National Park, reflecting its growing ecological significance and enhanced protection. Just four years later, in September 2022, the park entered global conservation history when eight African cheetahs from Namibia were released as part of Project Cheetah...
content: Overview of Kuno National Park Kuno National Park is one of India's most remarkable wildlife destinations, located in the Sheopur district of Madhya Pradesh, approximately 165 km from Gwalior. Named after the perennial Kuno River that flows through its heart, the park covers a core area of 748.76 square kilometres and forms part of the larger Kuno Wildlife Division. Originally designated as Kuno Wildlife Sanctuary in 1981, it was upgraded to National Park status in December 2018, making it one of Central India's most significant protected landscapes. Situated in the Vindhyan Hills, Kuno is a unique blend of tropical dry deciduous forests, open grasslands, riverine habitats and rugged hills. The landscape is dominated by Kardhai, Khair and Salai forests, interspersed with expansive meadows that provide excellent habitat for a wide variety of wildlife. Unlike many other protected areas in India, Kuno offers a rare combination of dense woodland and open savannah-like grasslands, creating ideal conditions for both predators and herbivores. The park supports an extraordinary diversity of wildlife. Visitors may encounter leopards, sloth bears, striped hyenas, Indian wolves, dholes, jackals and the world-famous African cheetahs. Large populations of chital, sambar, nilgai, chinkara, blackbuck and four-horned antelope provide a healthy prey base, while more than 200 bird species make Kuno an excellent destination for birdwatchers and wildlife photographers alike. Ancient forts such as the historic Palpur Fort, along with the scenic Kuno River, add a fascinating cultural dimension to the wilderness experience. {{image:1}} Today, Kuno National Park is internationally recognised as the home of Project Cheetah, India's ambitious programme to restore the cheetah after its extinction in the country over seven decades ago. Since the arrival of the first African cheetahs from Namibia in September 2022, followed by additional cheetahs from South Africa, the park has become a global symbol of wildlife restoration. In March 2023, female cheetah Jwala (Siyaya) gave birth to India's first cheetah cubs in over 70 years. The conservation milestone became even more significant in 2026 when KGP-2, an India-born female cheetah, gave birth to cubs in the wild—the first successful wild birth by a second-generation cheetah in India. These achievements have firmly established Kuno National Park as one of the world's most closely watched conservation landscapes. {{image:2}} History of Kuno National Park The forests of Kuno have been associated with wildlife conservation for centuries. Historical records from the former Gwalior State describe the region as a dense wilderness that once supported elephants, lions and a rich variety of native wildlife. During the early twentieth century, even Lord Curzon and Maharaja Madhavrao Scindia explored the possibility of reintroducing lions into this landscape, highlighting Kuno's long-standing ecological importance. Recognising the exceptional biodiversity of the region, the Government of Madhya Pradesh declared Kuno Wildlife Sanctuary in 1981 with an initial protected area of approximately 345 square kilometres. In 2002, an additional buffer area was added, expanding the protected landscape to strengthen wildlife conservation and habitat management. One of the most remarkable chapters in Kuno's history was the voluntary relocation of 24 villages between 1998 and 2003. More than 1,500 families were resettled outside the protected area, allowing over 6,000 hectares of habitat to regenerate naturally. This pioneering conservation effort transformed Kuno into one of India's best-prepared landscapes for the reintroduction of large carnivores and is widely regarded as one of the country's most successful habitat restoration programmes. {{image:3}} For many years, Kuno was identified by the Wildlife Institute of India as the most suitable location for establishing a second free-ranging population of Asiatic lions outside Gujarat. Although the lion translocation never materialised, the extensive habitat restoration, prey-base improvement and scientific management carried out for the project ultimately laid the foundation for another historic conservation initiative. title: Nearby Attractions in Kuno
author: Nived Yadav
excerpt: While Kuno National Park is best known for its incredible wildlife and India's famous Project Cheetah, the surrounding region is equally rich in history, spirituality and natural beauty. Whether you're...
content: While Kuno National Park is best known for its incredible wildlife and India's famous Project Cheetah, the surrounding region is equally rich in history, spirituality and natural beauty. Whether you're extending your safari holiday by a day or planning a week-long Central India tour, these nearby destinations perfectly complement your visit to Kuno. 1. Devkho Temple Distance from Kuno: Approximately 20 km (25 minutes) Hidden amidst the forests near Kuno National Park, Devkho Temple is one of the region's most peaceful spiritual destinations. Surrounded by rocky hills, dense forests and seasonal streams, this ancient temple offers visitors a tranquil atmosphere away from crowded tourist attractions. The scenic drive to Devkho is an experience in itself, making it an ideal stop before or after your jungle safari. During the monsoon, the lush greenery and flowing streams make the surroundings even more picturesque. Best for: Spiritual travellers, families, photographers and nature lovers. {{image:1}} 2. Madhav Tiger Reserve Distance from Kuno: Approximately 35 km (1 hour) Located near Shivpuri, Madhav Tiger Reserve is one of the best wildlife destinations to combine with a visit to Kuno National Park. The reserve is known for its scenic lakes, rolling grasslands and dry deciduous forests. Visitors have the opportunity to spot tigers, leopards, sloth bears, crocodiles, deer and an impressive variety of birdlife. Its landscape and safari experience are quite different from Kuno, making it an excellent addition to any wildlife itinerary. A combined Kuno–Madhav wildlife tour has become increasingly popular among wildlife photographers and nature enthusiasts looking to explore two of Central India's most exciting protected areas. {{image:2}} 3. Jal Mandir, Pohri Distance from Kuno: Approximately 20 km (30 minutes) Situated beside a picturesque water body, Jal Mandir in Pohri is one of the most beautiful religious sites near Kuno National Park. The peaceful surroundings and stunning reflections of the temple in the water create a perfect setting for relaxation and photography. Many visitors combine a visit to Jal Mandir with other nearby attractions in Pohri, making it an ideal half-day excursion from Kuno. {{image:3}} 4. Ganesh Temple, Pohri Distance from Kuno: Approximately 20 km (30 minutes) The famous Ganesh Temple at Pohri is one of the most revered temples in the Shivpuri district and attracts devotees from across the region throughout the year. Its religious significance, peaceful surroundings and easy accessibility make it a worthwhile stop while travelling between Kuno National Park, Pohri and Madhav Tiger Reserve. {{image:4}} 5. Gwalior Distance from Kuno: Approximately 160 km (2.5 hours) Gwalior is the nearest major city to Kuno National Park and serves as the primary gateway for many visitors arriving by air or train. The city is renowned for the magnificent Gwalior Fort, Jai Vilas Palace, Gujari Mahal Museum, Sas Bahu Temples and vibrant local markets. Spending a day exploring Gwalior before or after your safari adds a fascinating historical and cultural dimension to your wildlife holiday. {{image:5}} 6. Orchha Distance from Kuno: Approximately 280 km (5–5.5 hours) Situated on the banks of the Betwa River, Orchha is one of Madhya Pradesh's most picturesque heritage towns. Known for its magnificent palaces, cenotaphs, ancient temples and riverside charm, Orchha is a paradise for history enthusiasts, photographers and architecture lovers. Many travellers include Orchha in an extended itinerary covering Kuno National Park and Gwalior. {{image:6}} 7. Sawai Madhopur (Ranthambore National Park) Distance from Kuno: Approximately 170 km (2.5 hours) For wildlife enthusiasts wishing to experience another iconic tiger landscape, Sawai Madhopur is an excellent destination to combine with Kuno National Park. Home to the world-famous Ranthambore National Park, the area offers outstanding opportunities to photograph Bengal tigers, leopards, sloth bears and a variety of other wildlife. The historic Ranthambore Fort and ancient ruins further enhance the experience, making it a perfect addition to a Central India wildlife circuit. {{image:7}}
